questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its description.

pairs.right: Amount of matter; measured in kg
Force of gravity on an object; measured in N

questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is a force.

questions.prompt: What is the weight of a 50 kg student on Earth? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
What is the weight of the same 50 kg student on the Moon? (g = 1.6 N/kg)
questions.explain: 50 × 1.6 = 80 N: about one-sixth of the Earth weight.

questions.prompt: An astronaut’s mass on Earth is 70 kg. What is her mass on the Moon?

feedback.1: That’s thinking about weight. Mass doesn’t change from place to place.

questions.explain: Mass stays the same everywhere; only weight changes.

questions.prompt: A rover weighs 3710 N on Mars, where g = 3.71 N/kg. What is its mass?
On the Moon, an astronaut drops a hammer and a feather together. What happens?
questions.explain: With no air on the Moon, there is no air resistance, so gravity speeds both up equally.

questions.prompt: Order these worlds from the WEAKEST to the STRONGEST surface gravity.
questions.explain: Moon 1.6, Mars 3.7, Venus 8.9, Earth 9.8, Jupiter 24.8 N/kg.

questions.prompt: ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down near the Moon’s south pole in 2023. Explain why landing on the Moon needs rockets rather than parachutes, and how the Moon’s lower gravity helps.
questions.modelAnswer: Parachutes rely on air resistance, but the Moon has no atmosphere, so a parachute can’t slow the lander. Instead, thrusters fire downward to push against the fall. Because the Moon’s gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, the lander’s weight is much smaller, so less thrust and less fuel are needed to land gently.
rubric: No air, so parachutes cannot work
Rocket thrusters provide the upward force
Lower gravity means smaller weight, so less thrust or fuel
